I send around PDFs and markdown files to my coworkers so much and they use their agents to make sense of the world too, so I started using this skill methodology-appendix to make sure their agents could replicate what my agents found. 

---
name: methodology-appendix
description: "Every data-backed report or memo ends with a Methodology / Replication Appendix: the signal choice and its sensitivity, verbatim queries, derivation pseudocode over named constants, the rebuild command, and drift/limits. Appended by default, without asking."
---

# Methodology / Replication Appendix

## Rule

Any report, PDF or page whose conclusions rest on data queries ends with a
**Replication Appendix**. It is a working recipe, not a citation list. The test:

> A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate the document
> end to end from the appendix alone, without contacting the author.

If a reader would have to ask "which column did you use?", "what date was this
pulled?" or "how do I rebuild the PDF?", the appendix failed.

## Body voice

The body states conclusions plainly. No process narration ("I was asked...",
"on the first pass..."), no self-grading. The first sentence after the title
contains a finding. Everything about how you got there goes in the appendix at
the end, written for forensic recreation.

## When this fires

Always, automatically, for:
- analysis memos backed by database or API queries
- any PDF sent to partners, executives or external stakeholders
- pages presenting quantitative findings
- anything with tables of counts, rates or percentiles

Skip for narrative or qualitative writing, meeting notes, personal memos,
short ephemera, and documents with no data spine. Do not ask permission.

## The six sections

### 1. Header

```markdown
## Replication Appendix

A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate every number
and rebuild this document from this appendix alone.

**Access required:** <tool/CLI + auth, internal APIs>
**Snapshot date:** <ISO date>. Live-data documents won't reproduce exactly after this date; see Drift.
```

Once onchain comes out on the other side of this the systems will be almost impenetrable, which will be a very good thing long term, but that hardening can only come with time and by the best security teams reacting to the increasing complexity of attacks and recognising that every layer of the stack can be a weak point.

Perps platforms are still going to do extraordinarily well once we move past the "everything is going to get hacked" stage, and they are still the thing I am most bullish on.

Always prioritise survival so you can continually play another hand.

A few people read my recent post as a sign I’m no longer bullish on #uranium.

Nothing could be further from the truth.

I’m still as bullish as ever. This equity wipeout risks delaying financing for the very projects needed to meet future demand. The longer new supply gets pushed back, the more explosive the eventual price response will be.

When utilities start questioning whether there will be enough fuel for everyone, securing pounds will matter far more than the price paid.

I still believe uranium will trade well above $200/lb and that we will se many equities go 10x and more from current levels.

But a strong long-term thesis doesn’t protect a small sector from tax-loss selling and ETF rebalancing. Understanding those flows can make a huge difference to your portfolio.

Podcasts, TV shows, and seemingly everyone on Wall Street and X were celebrating Leopold Aschenbrenner as the new wunderkind, the genius who had supposedly figured out Wall Street and the future of AI.

Now, with hindsight, it’s easy for everyone to see the risks. But at the time, I was almost the only voice on X warning people to be extremely careful with this guy. His returns seemed astronomical, almost illogical. Something about the numbers simply didn’t add up.

For saying that, I received countless hate messages telling me how stupid I was, that I didn’t understand his genius, and that I was simply jealous of his success. Interestingly, looking back at my original post now, I see that most of those comments have conveniently been deleted. Typical X behavior.

I’m not jealous of anyone’s success. I wish everyone great success. But one thing I’m very good at is recognizing patterns.

Only in hindsight did we discover the extraordinary leverage behind those returns. Reports indicated that his fund was borrowing as much as $3 to $4 for every $1 of capital. What appeared to be extraordinary investment genius was also extraordinary risk-taking.

According to CNBC, Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund, Situational Awareness, reached $45 billion in assets at its peak before declining to around $10 billion. Its latest 13F shows just $1.58 billion in disclosed U.S. securities, although that figure does not represent the fund’s total assets.

And this goes far beyond Aschenbrenner. Just look at the latest 13F filings. Some of the most respected hedge funds on Wall Street were loading up on AI-related stocks, including $NVDA, during the third quarter, just before the recent selloff.

These are supposed to be the smartest people in the room, surrounded by the best analysts, researchers, and resources money can buy. Yet many were heavily exposed to the very sector that subsequently collapsed.

That’s the point. Nobody has a crystal ball. There are no saviors.

There is no Wall Street genius who has cracked the market. No AI wunderkind who has discovered the secret to investing. No growth stock promoter selling you a shortcut to becoming rich.

There is a reason not everyone is wealthy. Generating exceptional investment returns consistently over long periods is extraordinarily difficult. That’s how markets work.

Never confuse a short-term track record with genuine investment skill.

Someone who wins the lottery doesn’t suddenly become the smartest person in the room. And someone who delivers three spectacular years of returns hasn’t necessarily figured out Wall Street.

Time is the ultimate test. Not podcasts, not followers, not headlines, and certainly not three years of performance.

Indian law enforcement froze $3M from an innocent Chinese investor after mistaking a crypto bridge for a pig butchering scam. Now an Indian court has ordered Gate to hand his funds to a person they never belonged to.

My analysis of how Indian LE traced through an unlabeled service and wrongly froze @xxxkeym's Gate account:

The case stems from a pig butchering victim who allegedly lost $1.7M of BTC, USDT, DOGE & SOL in May 2025.

Andhra Pradesh CID registered it as Cr. No. 10/2025 and filed a charge sheet in March 2026.

In July 2025, xxxkeym had Gate deposit address 17mpajZ6Nq3dG3T6wUhaXxYF4Qy9HJnYx5 frozen after depositing 15 BTC from 3NcBhqK in the following transaction:
885f3afab562251b222363cf12095e864ddb94636674b01f0cdb05997e5a54a0

This is one transaction Indian LE cites in its notice. 3NcBhqK was funded by xxxkeym's own OKX & Binance withdrawals in Jan 2023 and the coins sat dormant for years until the Gate deposit. 

Indian LE never froze his OKX or Binance accounts, the actual source of the 15 BTC, which tells you how flawed their justification is.

Gate froze his entire account, which held roughly $3M at the time and about $1.5M today.

The Indian court order hands all of it to the complainant.

Gate deposit address 17mpajZ also received two deposits for 15 BTC total in 2025 from bc1pkkwqyxn3rm608ryuqg9hyqna0syq4jx5pxkr7pzg8n3usx6tyqfst5u966, which is also controlled by xxxkeym.

Shortly before the deposits to Gate, bc1pkkw was funded in three transactions by bc1quzwkggdf6ly06mrrnnled0qdr57w770k45n5n7 & bc1qtu66zfqxj6pam6e0zunwnggh87f5pjr7vdr5cd.

bc1quzw & bc1qtu66z were reported as alibarbit[.]bit, the same scam named in Indian LE's press release. 

That was a mistake. Both belong to the Merlin Chain bridge, which is unlabeled in most compliance tools. 

xxxkeym is simply a normal Merlin user trading tokens on the L2. This wrong label is the only place the scam touches his transaction history.

Below is the blockchain data showing each Merlin withdrawal by xxxkeym matched to a BTC payout from those addresses, plus screenshots of the bridge activity.

xxxkeym bridged 50 BTC into Merlin on March 28, 2024, over a year before the alleged May 2025 theft. 

His three withdrawals came out of that balance. I found zero onchain connections between xxxkeym and the theft.

Separately on July 15, 2025 xxxkeym had a 7 BTC private key compromise theft which was reported to local police and also SlowMist was engaged. His stolen funds flowed to Wasabi. 

This is embarrassing incompetence by Indian LE, who seem incapable of reviewing basic blockchain data.

Indian LE, the prosecutor and the judge all signed off on this, Gate froze the account, and LE did a full press release about it recently, while the real victim here (the Gate user) hasn't had access to his funds for nearly 16 months.

My hot take is VASPs need to challenge weak jurisdictions like India, Canada, etc due to repeated negligence in criminal cases.

AI data-centre: 100% moratorium improbable, modest slowdown likely and it will elongate the cycle (and the selloff has already priced a lot in)

Post-midterm noise has focused on local ballots, state pauses and talk of tighter rules on new data centres. Legitimate friction exists: power, water, permitting and community pushback are real constraints. However, a near-total U.S. halt is improbable as it will send the US into an immediate recession.

AI is a strategic priority; economic and geopolitical costs of freezing buildout are high. Much near-term capacity is already permitted or under construction.

Private land + evolving power solutions (gas, nuclear, efficiency) + international options provide outlets.

No federal ban has material traction; impact is more delay and higher cost than cancellation.

Base case from banks: some 2028 projects slide to 2029. This elongates the AI capex cycle rather than derailing it. Positives include:

1) Smoother supply-demand rebalancing (less boom-bust risk for the supply chain).

2) Better utilisation and pricing power for compute.

3) Improved credit outlook and more sustainable multi-year spending.

4) Hyperscalers still guiding strong near-term capex; and they will likely become FCF +ve

The aggressive selloff in AI infrastructure names (picks-and-shovels, semis, related industrials) has already discounted substantial slowdown risk. Multiples have compressed hard while order books and guidance have stayed firm. This looks more like a positioning/sentiment reset than a fundamental end of the cycle.

Quality AI infrastructure exposure still looks attractive if demand holds. Best to own companies with strong balance-sheets, high margins, FCF and real backlog. https://t.co/YKr5pL7G2c

More than 1.5 GW of chips are in China that shouldn’t be. Unwinding that web could reshape open-source AI.

“In our view, there’s more than one and a half gigawatts of chips in China that are not supposed to be there according to US law. How they get there, that whole web, that’s what’s going to unwind.”

“If NVIDIA can no longer support the open-source ecosystem, because that was Jensen’s primary goal, does that mean the open-source ecosystem falls away?”

“Now open source looks a lot weaker with NVIDIA down and out. Anthropic looks much more likely to get a complete monopoly or a duopoly. This bodes really well for Anthropic’s IPO next week.”

“They’re more diverse in what chips they use than any other company in the world.”
